t: Rearrange K Substrings to Form Target String — Multiset of Chunks
o: We split `s` into exactly k consecutive chunks of equal length n/k, and we may reorder those chunks (but not rearrange characters inside a chunk) to try to build `t`. So the question reduces to: does the multiset of chunks of `s` equal the multiset of chunks of `t`? In Example 1, s splits into ["ab","cd"] and t into ["cd","ab"] — same multiset, so true. In Example 3 with k=2 the chunks are length 3: s gives ["aab","bcc"], t gives ["bba","acc"] — different multisets, so false. Since n can be 2·10^5 and k up to n, any approach that compares all pairs of chunks is too slow; hashing or sorting chunk strings in O(n) / O(n log n) total is required.
k: Chunk boundaries are fixed: chunk i of s must match some chunk of t exactly (characters cannot move across chunk borders).
The answer is simply whether the multiset of s's chunks equals the multiset of t's chunks.
Hashing each chunk (or rolling hashes) lets us compare multisets in linear time instead of O(n·n/k) string comparisons.

a.i: Split both strings into their k chunks and store them in two lists. For each chunk of s, find an unused matching chunk of t by scanning; if every chunk is matched, return true. This directly mirrors the problem definition but costs quadratic time when there are many small chunks.
s: Let m = len(s)/k be the chunk length; split s and t into lists of chunks.
For each s-chunk, scan unused t-chunks for an exact string match; mark it used.
If some s-chunk has no match, return false; otherwise return true.
a.t: O(n · k) worst case — each of the k s-chunks may scan all k t-chunks with O(m) comparisons each.

a.n: Approach 2: Hash Map Counting of Chunk Strings (Optimal)
a.i: Since only reordering chunks is allowed, s can form t iff every chunk of t appears among the chunks of s with matching multiplicity. Put all chunks of s into a hash map counting occurrences, then subtract counts while scanning chunks of t; any mismatch means impossible. Each chunk comparison is O(m), done once per chunk, giving linear total work.
s: Build a Counter/hash map of all k chunks of s.
Iterate over the k chunks of t, decrementing counts; if a chunk is missing or its count hits zero, return false.
Return true if all chunks of t were consumed successfully.
a.t: O(n) expected time — building and querying the map touches each character a constant number of times (hashing each chunk is O(m)).
a.sp: O(n) — the map stores up to k chunk keys totaling n characters.

a.i: Two multisets are equal iff their sorted sequences are identical. Split both strings into chunk lists, sort each list lexicographically, and compare element by element. This avoids hash maps at the cost of a log factor from sorting.
s: Compute m = len(s)/k and extract the k chunks of s and of t.
Compare the two sorted lists position by position; return true iff they are identical.
a.t: O(n log k) — extracting chunks is O(n); sorting k strings of length m costs O(k · m log k) = O(n log k) comparisons.

w: In an interview, lead with the multiset observation and implement Approach 2 (hash map counting) — it's optimal, simple, and easy to explain; mention Approach 3 as a clean alternative if you prefer avoiding hash maps. Pitfalls: forgetting that chunk length is n/k (not fixed), confusing 'rearrange substrings' with permuting characters inside chunks (characters never cross chunk boundaries), and off-by-one errors in substring slicing. Edge cases: k = n (all chunks single characters — reduces to checking anagram, guaranteed true here), k = 1 (answer is always true since s and t are given as anagrams... actually k=1 requires s == t exactly, since no reordering is possible — verify this!). Follow-ups: what if you could also reverse individual chunks (then compare canonical forms min(chunk, reversed(chunk))), or what if k didn't divide n?
